transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I just... I don't feel like myself anymore, you know? It's like the engine's running but the car won't go into gear. I used to do a lot. I'd go hiking up the ridge every weekend, coached my nephew's little league team—they had these bright green jerseys this year, terrible color, really washed the kids out, but they played hard. I even played guitar, mostly acoustic stuff, some old folk songs my dad taught me. He had this vintage Martin, beautiful sound, smelled like cedar and old tobacco. But now... I stopped all of it. I don't play, I don't hike, I don't even call people back. The phone rings and I just look at it. Some days I just sit in my small rental for hours. I know there are things I should be doing, dishes, laundry, whatever, but I just... I can't make myself start. It's like I'm glued to the chair. Did you know the guy who invented the reclining chair was a dentist? Makes sense, I guess. But yeah, I just sit there.
Do you still enjoy the things you used to do, or has the pleasure gone away?

I... I'm not really sure if the feeling is gone, because I haven't actually tried to do any of it. So I don't know if the pleasure is still there or not. Like the guitar, I haven't even opened the case in months. The strings are probably all rusted out by now. 

Rust is a relentless thing, you know? Just oxidation, but it ruins everything. We had this massive problem with rust on our patrol vehicles at work. I do protective services for the county, mostly driving the perimeter of the reservoir and the water treatment plants. We had these heavy-duty white SUVs, and the road salt in the winter would just eat right through the undercarriage. You'd think having a bachelor's degree would mean I wouldn't be the one out there on my hands and knees inspecting wheel wells, but you just end up doing whatever needs doing out in the cold. 

One year, the county decided to use this beet juice mixture on the icy roads instead of salt to save the metal. It made the whole valley smell like rotten soup. The deer loved it, though. They'd come right up to the asphalt and just lick the yellow lines. Had to brake for them constantly. 

But... I'm sorry, what did you ask? About enjoying things? Yeah, I just... I don't really know. I haven't noticed one way or the other.
Do you feel like you would enjoy doing those things, like hiking or playing guitar, if you were actually doing them?

I don't know... I mean, maybe? But I just can't get myself to even try. Like I was saying, I just don't feel like myself anymore. I stopped hiking, stopped coaching, stopped playing the guitar... I don't even call people back. I just sit in that small rental for hours. I know there are things to do, but I just can't make myself start. 

It's like when you're trying to start a fire with damp wood. You can strike a match all you want, but it just fizzles out. I used to build these massive bonfires down by the lake when I was younger. We'd gather all the driftwood that washed up after a storm. Some of those pieces were huge, like whole tree trunks. You'd need three guys just to drag them up the beach. The trick was to start small, lots of dry kindling, maybe some pine needles. Pine needles burn hot and fast, you know? They smell incredible, too. Like Christmas, but sharper. 

We used to roast marshmallows until they were completely black on the outside, just pure carbon. My brother always liked his lightly browned, but I wanted mine charred. He moved out to Oregon a few years back. Works in a lumber mill now, ironically enough. He says the rain out there is different. It doesn't just fall; it kind of hangs in the air like a mist. 

But yeah... I don't know if I'd enjoy the guitar or the hiking if I tried. I just... I sit there and I can't start.
Do you think you would feel any pleasure if you were to start doing something you used to enjoy, like playing the guitar?

I feel like you're asking me the exact same thing again, Doc. Like I've been saying, mostly I just don't feel like myself anymore. I stopped hiking, coaching, playing guitar, calling people back... all of it. Some days I just sit in that small rental for hours, knowing there are things I need to do, but I just can't make myself start. 

When you sit in one spot for that long, you really start to notice the walls. The paint in my place is this awful off-white, they call it 'eggshell' I think. But eggshells are actually incredibly strong if you squeeze them from the top and bottom. It's the arch structure. The Romans figured that out with the aqueducts. They moved millions of gallons of water using just gravity and arches. Water always finds the lowest point, no matter what. That's why the reservoir I patrol is down in the valley. The fog rolls off the water in the mornings and gets so thick you can't even see the hood of your own truck. It's like driving through a cloud. Clouds are just water vapor anyway, but they look so solid from the ground. Like you could just lie down on them.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in things you used to find pleasurable?

Doc, are you testing my memory or something? I feel like we're just going in circles here. Yes, I've lost interest. Like I just told you, I really just don't feel like myself at all anymore. I dropped everything—the hiking, the coaching, the guitar. I don't even pick up the phone to call people back anymore. I literally just sit in my small rental for hours on end. My brain knows there are things I need to do, but I just can't make myself start them. 

I used to really like the coaching, though. Youth baseball. The geometry of a baseball diamond is actually pretty incredible if you look at the math of it. The bases are exactly 90 feet apart, which is the exact perfect distance to make a ground ball to the infield a dead tie between the runner and the throw. Whoever figured that out understood spatial relations perfectly. 

Space is mostly empty anyway, you know. Even the atoms in our bodies are something like 99 percent empty space. So when you're sitting in your chair right now, you aren't actually touching it. Your electrons are just repelling the chair's electrons. You're technically just hovering on an electromagnetic field. Magnets are fascinating. The whole earth is just a giant magnet because of the molten iron core spinning around down there. If that core ever stopped spinning, we'd lose our magnetic field and the solar wind would just strip our atmosphere right off into space. Just like Mars. Mars used to have oceans, they think. But now it's just red dust. Red dust gets everywhere, worse than rust.
Do you feel sad most of the time?

Sad? No, I wouldn't say I feel sad. I don't really feel much of anything, to be honest. I'm not sitting around crying or feeling miserable like that. Crying is just a weird biological response anyway, if you think about it. Your lacrimal glands just start pumping out saline solution to flush out the eye. It's basically just salt water. The salinity of human tears is actually really close to the ocean. We basically carry little oceans around inside our heads. 

The ocean has these deep thermal vents where water gets superheated by the earth's magma, but it doesn't boil because the pressure down there is so intense. There are whole ecosystems at the bottom of the sea that survive completely without sunlight. They use chemosynthesis instead of photosynthesis. Just these giant tube worms and blind crabs living in total, absolute darkness. Darkness is really just the absence of photons. 

When I'm doing night patrols out at the reservoir, it gets so dark out there you can't even see your own hand in front of your face. You have to rely on the rods in your eyes instead of the cones. Cones are for color, but rods pick up movement and low light. That's why if you look slightly to the side of something in the dark, you can actually see it better. Peripheral vision is an ancient survival trait. Our ancestors needed it to see predators sneaking up on them in the tall grass. Grass is actually one of the most successful plant species on the entire planet. It grows on every continent, even Antarctica now because the ice is melting. The glaciers are retreating by feet every year. It's just solid ice turning back into water and finding the lowest point again.
Do you often feel guilty about anything?

Guilty? No, I don't... I don't think I feel guilty about anything. I mean, I'm not doing anything wrong, just sitting in my place. But it's funny you mention guilt, because in the legal system, guilt has to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. That's a huge burden of proof. The whole justice system is based on this idea of weighing evidence on scales, like Lady Justice. She wears a blindfold so she's impartial. 

Blindfolds remind me of how they used to train falcons back in the Middle Ages. They'd put these tiny leather hoods over the birds' heads to keep them calm. Falconry was the sport of kings. The birds have incredible eyesight, they can spot a mouse from hundreds of feet up in the air. Their eyes are actually so big they take up most of the space in their skulls, which means they can't really move their eyes around like we do. They have to turn their whole head. Owls are like that too. They can turn their heads almost all the way around because they have extra vertebrae in their necks. 

The human spine only has seven cervical vertebrae. It's the same number as a giraffe, surprisingly. A giraffe's neck is just stretched out, but the bone count is exactly the same. Bone is a fascinating material. It's a composite, mostly calcium phosphate and collagen. It's actually stronger than concrete, ounce for ounce. Concrete is what they used to build the dam at the reservoir I patrol. Millions of tons of it holding back all that water. If that dam ever gave way, the sheer force of the water would wipe out everything in the valley in minutes. Water is heavy. A gallon weighs over eight pounds. So when you think about millions of gallons... that's a lot of weight pressing against the concrete.
Do you feel tired most of the time?

Tired? Yeah, I guess I'm pretty tired. I mean, I sleep a lot, but I don't really wake up feeling refreshed or anything. It's more like this heavy, dragging feeling all the time. Heaviness is an interesting concept, really. It's just gravity pulling mass toward the center of the earth. Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces in physics, which is wild when you think about it because it holds the whole universe together. 

The other forces are electromagnetism, and the strong and weak nuclear forces. The strong nuclear force is what holds the nucleus of an atom together. If you split that nucleus, you get nuclear fission. That's how atomic bombs work, or nuclear power plants. Power plants generate electricity by spinning turbines, usually with steam. Steam is just water in a gaseous state. When water boils, it expands by something like 1,700 times its liquid volume. That expansion creates a massive amount of pressure. Pressure is what makes diamonds out of carbon deep underground. Diamonds are the hardest natural substance on earth, but you can actually shatter them with a hammer if you hit them at the right angle because of their cleavage planes. 

Cleavage planes are just the weak points in the crystal lattice. Everything has a weak point, structurally speaking. Even steel bridges. That's why engineers have to account for resonance frequencies. If the wind blows at just the right speed and matches the bridge's natural frequency, the whole thing can start swinging and eventually collapse. Like that bridge in Washington state back in the 40s. Galloping Gertie, they called it. The wind just tore it apart like it was made of rubber. Rubber comes from trees originally, mostly in South America. They tap the trees for sap, kind of like maple syrup. Maple syrup takes about 40 gallons of sap just to make one gallon of syrup. It's a huge reduction process. Boiling things down to their essence.
Have you noticed any change in your appetite?

Appetite? I haven't really noticed a change, I don't think. I just eat whatever's around when I'm supposed to. Food is mostly just fuel anyway, you know? Like putting gas in a car. Gasoline is actually a really complex mixture of hydrocarbons. They refine it from crude oil by heating it up in these massive distillation columns. The lighter molecules rise to the top, and the heavier ones sink to the bottom. That's how you get everything from jet fuel down to asphalt. 

Asphalt is what they use to pave most of the roads around here. It's flexible, which is why it handles the freeze-thaw cycle better than concrete. When water freezes, it expands by about nine percent. That's why pipes burst in the winter if they aren't insulated properly. Insulation works by trapping little pockets of air. Air is a terrible conductor of heat, which makes it a great insulator. That's how double-pane windows work. They just trap a layer of argon gas between two sheets of glass. 

Glass is technically an amorphous solid. It's not a true solid, but it's not a liquid either. The molecules are just frozen in a disordered state. It's made by melting sand, mostly silica. You have to heat it to almost three thousand degrees Fahrenheit to get it to melt. Lightning can actually do that naturally. When lightning strikes a sandy beach, it fuses the sand into these hollow glass tubes called fulgurites. They look like frozen lightning bolts buried in the ground. Lightning is just a massive discharge of static electricity. The voltage is so high it literally rips electrons off the air molecules, turning the air into plasma. Plasma is the fourth state of matter. Most of the universe is actually made of plasma, like the sun and all the stars. Stars are basically just giant, continuous fusion explosions held together by their own gravity.
Have you ever thought about harming yourself?

Harming myself? No, no I haven't thought about that. I just do my patrols, you know? Keep an eye on things. Keeping an eye on things is important, especially at night. Night vision is a fascinating biological adaptation. Humans have terrible night vision compared to most predators. We rely mostly on the cone cells in our retinas for color and detail, but we don't have enough rod cells to see well in the dark. 

Cats, on the other hand, have a tapetum lucidum. It's this reflective layer behind their retina that bounces light back through the eye a second time. That's why their eyes glow in the dark when a flashlight hits them. Flashlights used to run on incandescent bulbs, with a tiny tungsten filament inside. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any pure metal. They use it in rocket engine nozzles because it can withstand the extreme heat of the exhaust gases. 

Rockets work on Newton's third law of motion—for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. It's the same principle as letting the air out of a balloon. Balloons are usually made of latex, which is incredibly stretchy. But if you blow them up too much, the surface tension gets too high and they pop. Surface tension is what allows water striders to walk on the surface of a pond without sinking. The water molecules at the surface cohere so tightly they form a sort of invisible film. It's the same reason water forms into spherical droplets when it falls. Spheres are the most efficient shape in nature because they have the smallest surface area for a given volume. That's why planets are round. They just pull themselves into a sphere under their own gravitational weight as they form.
Do you find it difficult to initiate physical activity or movements?

Initiating movement? Yeah, I guess. Mostly I just don't feel like myself anymore—I stopped hiking, coaching, playing guitar, and calling people back, and some days I sit in that small rental for hours knowing there are things to do but I can't make myself start. 

Starting requires overcoming static friction. Static friction is the force that keeps an object at rest, and it's always stronger than kinetic friction, which is the force that opposes an object that's already moving. That's why it takes so much more effort to get a heavy box sliding than it does to keep it sliding. Friction is just caused by the microscopic roughness of surfaces. Even something that feels perfectly smooth, like a mirror, is actually full of jagged peaks and valleys if you look at it under an electron microscope. 

Electron microscopes use a beam of accelerated electrons instead of light to illuminate a specimen. Because the wavelength of an electron can be up to a hundred thousand times shorter than visible light photons, they have incredible resolving power. Photons are elementary particles that carry the electromagnetic force. They have no rest mass, which is why they can travel at the speed of light. The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 meters per second. It's the ultimate cosmic speed limit. 

According to Einstein's theory of special relativity, as an object with mass accelerates closer to the speed of light, its relativistic mass increases and it requires exponentially more energy to keep accelerating. That's why time dilation happens. If you were traveling on a ship near the speed of light, time would pass much slower for you compared to people back on Earth. Earth is the only planet in our solar system not named after a Greek or Roman deity. The name just comes from Old English and Germanic words for ground or soil. Soil is actually a living ecosystem. A single teaspoon of healthy soil can contain more microorganisms than there are people on the entire planet.
Do you have trouble concentrating?

Concentrating? I haven't really noticed a problem with that, no. I mean, I can focus when I need to. Focus is really just about filtering out the background noise, right? Like how a camera lens adjusts to bring a specific subject into sharp relief while blurring out the background. That's called depth of field. It depends on the aperture size. A wider aperture gives you a shallower depth of field, which is great for portraits. 

Portraits used to be painted by hand, which took hours, sometimes days of sitting perfectly still. Before photography, that was the only way to capture someone's likeness. The first permanent photograph was taken by Joseph Nicéphore Niépce in 1826. It took an eight-hour exposure time just to capture the view from his window. Silver halides are the light-sensitive chemicals they used in early film photography. When light hits the silver halide crystals, it creates a latent image that you have to develop in a darkroom using chemical baths. 

Chemical baths have to be kept at a very specific temperature, usually around 68 degrees Fahrenheit, for the developer to work correctly. Temperature is just a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance. The faster the molecules are moving, the hotter it feels. That's why boiling water bubbles—the water molecules at the bottom get so much energy from the heat source that they turn into a gas and rise to the surface. Water boils at 212 degrees Fahrenheit at sea level, but the boiling point drops as you go up in elevation because the atmospheric pressure is lower. 

Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the air pressing down on everything. At sea level, it's about 14.7 pounds per square inch. You don't feel it because the pressure inside your body is pushing outward with the exact same force. It's like how deep-sea fish don't get crushed by the weight of the ocean above them. Some of those fish down in the Mariana Trench are incredible. They have bioluminescent lures hanging off their heads to attract prey in the pitch black. Bioluminescence is a chemical reaction that produces light without heat, usually involving a molecule called luciferin and an enzyme called luciferase. Fireflies use the exact same chemical process to signal each other in the summer.
Do you find it hard to get out of bed in the morning?

Get out of bed? Yeah, I mean... it's like I said before. I just don't feel like myself anymore. I used to be up at dawn, hiking, coaching, playing guitar... calling people back. Now some days I just sit in that small rental for hours. I know there are things to do, but I just can't make myself start. It's like my battery is completely drained. 

Batteries are fascinating, really. The first true battery was the Voltaic pile, invented by Alessandro Volta in 1800. He stacked alternating discs of zinc and copper, separated by cloth soaked in saltwater. Saltwater is a great conductor of electricity because the sodium and chloride ions dissociate in the water, allowing electrons to flow freely. That's why you should never swim in the ocean during a thunderstorm. Lightning strikes the water and the current spreads out over a huge area. 

Lightning is just a massive electrostatic discharge. It happens when the negative charges in the bottom of a storm cloud build up so much that they overcome the insulating properties of the air and connect with the positive charges on the ground. The air around a lightning channel can heat up to 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit, which is five times hotter than the surface of the sun. The sun is a G-type main-sequence star, mostly made of hydrogen and helium. It generates energy through nuclear fusion in its core, where the pressure and temperature are so high that hydrogen atoms are squeezed together to form helium. 

Helium is the second most abundant element in the universe, but it's actually relatively rare on Earth. Most of the helium we use for balloons and MRI machines is extracted from natural gas deposits deep underground. Natural gas is a fossil fuel, formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient marine microorganisms that sank to the bottom of the ocean and were buried under layers of sediment. The pressure and heat over time slowly cooked that organic matter into hydrocarbons. Hydrocarbons are the basis of all organic chemistry. Carbon is unique because it has four valence electrons, meaning it can form four strong covalent bonds with other atoms, creating incredibly complex molecular structures like DNA. DNA is the blueprint of life, a double helix structure discovered by Watson, Crick, and Rosalind Franklin.
Do you feel motivated to make changes in your life?

Motivated to change? I mean, it's... it's like I've been telling you. I just don't feel like myself anymore. I sit in that small rental for hours, and I know I should make changes, I know there are things to do, but I just can't make myself start. All that stuff I used to do—the hiking, coaching, the guitar, calling people—it's just gone. It's like an engine with a bad starter motor. 

Starter motors are basically just direct current electric motors that engage with the flywheel to turn the engine over. Once the crankshaft is spinning, the pistons can start drawing in the air-fuel mixture for the internal combustion process. Most cars use a four-stroke engine based on the Otto cycle, which is intake, compression, power, and exhaust. 

The power stroke is where the spark plug fires, creating a tiny controlled explosion that forces the piston back down the cylinder. An explosion is really just a rapid increase in volume and release of energy, usually with the generation of high temperatures and gases. The first chemical explosive was black powder, invented by Chinese alchemists in the 9th century. They were actually trying to find an elixir for immortality when they mixed saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal. 

Charcoal is made through pyrolysis, which is the thermal decomposition of organic material at elevated temperatures in an inert atmosphere. You have to heat the wood without oxygen, otherwise it just combusts and turns into ash. Ash is mostly composed of calcium, potassium, and magnesium trace minerals. Potassium is an alkali metal, and it's highly reactive. If you drop pure potassium into water, it reacts violently, producing hydrogen gas and enough heat to instantly ignite the hydrogen. 

Hydrogen is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe, making up about 75 percent of all normal matter. It's the primary fuel for the nuclear fusion reactions in stars. When stars run out of hydrogen in their core, they start fusing heavier elements like helium, carbon, and oxygen, all the way up to iron. Fusing iron actually absorbs energy instead of releasing it, which causes the star's core to suddenly collapse under its own gravity, leading to a massive supernova explosion. Supernovas are so bright they can outshine an entire galaxy for a few weeks.
Do you find yourself moving or reacting more slowly than you used to?

Reacting more slowly? No, it's... it's actually the opposite. On patrol I started reacting before I could slow myself down, like crouching behind counters, signaling people to get back, repeating their last words to check if they were part of it. I was just pacing the same route over and over until staff looked scared of me. Pacing is just a repetitive locomotive pattern. Human locomotion is bipedal, which is actually incredibly rare in the animal kingdom. 

Bipedalism freed up our upper limbs so early hominids could carry things and use tools. The first stone tools were made during the Lower Paleolithic era by striking rocks together to create sharp flakes, a technique called flintknapping. Flint is a type of chert, which is a hard, fine-grained sedimentary rock composed mostly of microcrystalline quartz. Quartz is the second most abundant mineral in Earth's continental crust, right behind feldspar. 

Quartz is fascinating because it's piezoelectric, meaning it generates an electrical charge when mechanical stress is applied to it. That's why quartz crystals are used in watches to keep precise time. A tiny battery sends a current through the crystal, making it oscillate at exactly 32,768 times per second. A second is officially defined by the International System of Units as the time it takes a cesium-133 atom to oscillate over nine billion times. Cesium is an alkali metal with a melting point of only 83.3 degrees Fahrenheit, which means a solid chunk of it can literally melt in the palm of your hand. 

The human body maintains a core temperature of about 98.6 degrees, which is regulated by the hypothalamus in the brain. The brain is the most energy-demanding organ in the body. It uses about 20 percent of your total calorie intake despite only making up about two percent of your total body weight. Most of that energy goes into maintaining the electrical charge across the membranes of neurons so they can fire action potentials.
Do you feel like your thoughts are slower than they used to be?

Thoughts slower? No, it's... I wouldn't say that. I haven't really noticed them slowing down. If anything, they just jump around all the time, like a radio constantly scanning through stations trying to lock onto a frequency. 

Frequencies are measured in hertz, which is named after Heinrich Hertz, the physicist who first conclusively proved the existence of electromagnetic waves in the 1880s. He used a spark gap transmitter to generate radio waves in his laboratory. Radio waves have the longest wavelengths in the electromagnetic spectrum, which also includes microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays. 

Gamma rays are the most energetic form of light and are produced by the hottest and most volatile objects in the universe, like neutron stars and pulsars. A pulsar is a highly magnetized rotating neutron star that emits beams of electromagnetic radiation out of its magnetic poles. Because the star is spinning, if those beams sweep past Earth, we see them as regular pulses of light, kind of like a lighthouse. 

Lighthouses were historically used to mark dangerous coastlines and guide ships safely into harbor. The most famous one was the Lighthouse of Alexandria, built by the Ptolemaic Kingdom in ancient Egypt. It was estimated to be at least 330 feet tall, making it one of the tallest man-made structures in the world for many centuries before it was destroyed by earthquakes. Most of those ancient structures were built using limestone, which is a sedimentary rock composed largely of the minerals calcite and aragonite. Both of those are different crystal forms of calcium carbonate, which is the exact same stuff that makes up the shells of marine organisms like snails, oysters, and corals. Coral reefs are some of the most diverse ecosystems on the planet, often called the rainforests of the sea because they provide a home for about a quarter of all marine species despite taking up less than one percent of the ocean floor.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight recently?

Weight changes? I... I don't think so. I haven't really been paying attention to the scale or anything. I mean, my clothes still fit the same as they always have, so I'm pretty sure my mass has stayed constant. Mass is an intrinsic property of matter, whereas weight is actually just the force exerted on an object by gravity. 

Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces of nature, the others being electromagnetism, the strong nuclear force, and the weak nuclear force. The strong force is what holds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus of an atom. It has to be incredibly strong to overcome the electromagnetic repulsion between the positively charged protons. Protons are made up of two up quarks and one down quark, held together by elementary particles called gluons. 

Gluons mediate the strong force, and their interactions are described by the theory of quantum chromodynamics. In quantum chromodynamics, quarks have a property called "color charge," which can be red, green, or blue. But they don't actually have color; physicists just used those terms because the math for how they combine is similar to how primary colors of light combine to make white. White light contains all the visible wavelengths of the spectrum, which Isaac Newton famously demonstrated in 1666 by using a glass prism to split sunlight into a rainbow. 

A rainbow is an optical phenomenon caused by refraction, internal reflection, and dispersion of light in water droplets resulting in a continuous spectrum of light appearing in the sky. It takes the form of a multicolored circular arc, though we usually only see a semicircle from the ground. The only way to see a full circle rainbow is from an airplane or a high mountain peak where you can look down at the water droplets suspended in the air. Air is a mixture of gases, primarily nitrogen, which makes up about 78 percent of the Earth's atmosphere, and oxygen, which is about 21 percent. Nitrogen is essential for all living things because it's a key component of amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins.
Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure from activities that you once enjoyed?

Pleasure? Mostly I just... I don't feel like myself anymore. I stopped hiking, coaching, playing guitar, and calling people back. Some days I just sit in that small rental for hours, knowing there are things to do, but I just can't make myself start. The guitar just sits there in its case. Guitars are chordophones, meaning they produce sound by the vibration of strings. That vibration is transferred through the bridge to the soundboard, which moves the air and creates acoustic energy. 

Sound is basically just a longitudinal wave consisting of compressions and rarefactions traveling through a medium. In dry air at 68 degrees Fahrenheit, sound travels at approximately 343 meters per second, or about 767 miles per hour. If an object exceeds that speed, it breaks the sound barrier, producing a continuous shock wave known as a sonic boom. The first manned aircraft to officially break the sound barrier in level flight was the Bell X-1, piloted by Chuck Yeager in 1947. 

The X-1 was actually modeled after a .50-caliber bullet because engineers knew that specific shape was aerodynamically stable at supersonic speeds. A standard bullet is propelled by the rapid expansion of gases from burning smokeless powder, which replaced black powder in the late 19th century. Black powder is a chemical mixture of sulfur, charcoal, and potassium nitrate, which was historically known as saltpeter. 

Potassium nitrate is heavily used today in agriculture as a fertilizer because it provides two major macronutrients that plants need to survive: potassium and nitrogen. Potassium is an alkali metal, and it's incredibly reactive. If you drop a piece of pure potassium into a bowl of water, it reacts instantly and violently, producing hydrogen gas and generating enough heat to ignite that gas, which burns with a characteristic pale purple flame. Fire itself isn't a state of matter; it's just the visible, tangible effect of the process of combustion, which is a high-temperature exothermic redox chemical reaction between a fuel and an oxidant.
Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure from activities that you once enjoyed?

Pleasure? I... I don't know if pleasure is the right word. I just don't feel like myself anymore. I used to do a lot, you know? Hiking, coaching, playing guitar... calling people back. Now I just stopped. Some days I just sit in that small rental for hours. I know there are things to do, but I just can't make myself start. It's like an engine that won't turn over. 

Engines, especially internal combustion engines, rely on a starter motor to get the crankshaft turning. The starter motor is an electric motor that draws a massive amount of current from the car's battery. Batteries store chemical energy and convert it into electrical energy through redox reactions. The most common type of battery in cars is the lead-acid battery, which was invented in 1859 by French physicist Gaston Planté. It's the oldest type of rechargeable battery. 

Rechargeable batteries are essential for modern electronics, like smartphones and laptops, which mostly use lithium-ion technology. Lithium is the lightest metal and the least dense solid element under standard conditions. It's highly reactive and flammable, which is why lithium fires are so dangerous and hard to put out. You can't just use water because water reacts with lithium to produce hydrogen gas, which just fuels the fire even more. Hydrogen is the most abundant chemical substance in the universe, constituting roughly 75 percent of all baryonic mass. Stars, like our sun, are primarily composed of hydrogen in its plasma state. 

Plasma is one of the four fundamental states of matter, along with solid, liquid, and gas. It's an ionized gas consisting of positive ions and free electrons in proportions resulting in more or less no overall electric charge. Because it's ionized, plasma is highly electrically conductive and responds strongly to electromagnetic fields. The Northern Lights, or Aurora Borealis, are a beautiful natural display of plasma in the Earth's magnetosphere, caused by solar wind interacting with the Earth's magnetic field. The magnetic field protects us from that solar wind, which would otherwise strip away the ozone layer that protects the Earth from harmful ultraviolet radiation.
Have you had any thoughts of self-harm or suicide recently?

Harm myself? No... no, I haven't had any thoughts like that. I don't want to die. I've spent my whole career trying to keep people safe from harm, actually. When you're trying to prevent bodily harm on the job, you rely a lot on personal protective equipment, especially Kevlar vests. Kevlar is incredibly strong. It was actually invented by a chemist named Stephanie Kwolek back in 1965 while she was working for DuPont. 

She was trying to find a lightweight, strong fiber to use in tires, but she ended up creating this synthetic polymer that's five times stronger than steel on an equal weight basis. Cesium is an alkali metal with a melting point of only 83.3 degrees Fahrenheit, which means a solid chunk of it can literally melt in the palm of your hand. 

The human body maintains a core temperature of about 98.6 degrees, which is regulated by the hypothalamus in the brain. The brain is the most energy-demanding organ in the body. It uses about 20 percent of your total calorie intake despite only making up about two percent of your total body weight. Most of that energy goes into maintaining the electrical charge across the membranes of neurons so they can fire action potentials.

Frequencies are measured in hertz, which is named after Heinrich Hertz, the physicist who first conclusively proved the existence of electromagnetic waves in the 1880s. He used a spark gap transmitter to generate radio waves in his laboratory. Radio waves have the longest wavelengths in the electromagnetic spectrum, which also includes microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays. 

Gamma rays are the most energetic form of light and are produced by the hottest and most volatile objects in the universe, like neutron stars and pulsars. A pulsar is a highly magnetized rotating neutron star that emits beams of electromagnetic radiation out of its magnetic poles. Because the star is spinning, if those beams sweep past Earth, we see them as regular pulses of light, kind of like a lighthouse. 

Lighthouses were historically used to mark dangerous coastlines and guide ships safely into harbor. The most famous one was the Lighthouse of Alexandria, built by the Ptolemaic Kingdom in ancient Egypt. It was estimated to be at least 330 feet tall, making it one of the tallest man-made structures in the world for many centuries before it was destroyed by earthquakes. Most of those ancient structures were built using limestone, which is a sedimentary rock composed largely of the minerals calcite and aragonite. Both of those are different crystal forms of calcium carbonate, which is the exact same stuff that makes up the shells of marine organisms like snails, oysters, and corals. Coral reefs are some of the most diverse ecosystems on the planet, often called the rainforests of the sea because they provide a home for about a quarter of all marine species despite taking up less than one percent of the ocean floor.

Mass is an intrinsic property of matter, whereas weight is actually just the force exerted on an object by gravity. 

Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces of nature, the others being electromagnetism, the strong nuclear force, and the weak nuclear force. The strong force is what holds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus of an atom. It has to be incredibly strong to overcome the electromagnetic repulsion between the positively charged protons. Protons are made up of two up quarks and one down quark, held together by elementary particles called gluons. 

Gluons mediate the strong force, and their interactions are described by the theory of quantum chromodynamics. In quantum chromodynamics, quarks have a property called "color charge," which can be red, green, or blue. But they don't actually have color; physicists just used those terms because the math for how they combine is similar to how primary colors of light combine to make white. White light contains all the visible wavelengths of the spectrum, which Isaac Newton famously demonstrated in 1666 by using a glass prism to split sunlight into a rainbow. 

A rainbow is an optical phenomenon caused by refraction, internal reflection, and dispersion of light in water droplets resulting in a continuous spectrum of light appearing in the sky. It takes the form of a multicolored circular arc, though we usually only see a semicircle from the ground. The only way to see a full circle rainbow is from an airplane or a high mountain peak where you can look down at the water droplets suspended in the air. Air is a mixture of gases, primarily nitrogen, which makes up about 78 percent of the Earth's atmosphere, and oxygen, which is about 21 percent. Guitars are chordophones, meaning they produce sound by the vibration of strings. That vibration is transferred through the bridge to the soundboard, which moves the air and creates acoustic energy. 

Sound is basically just a longitudinal wave consisting of compressions and rarefactions traveling through a medium. In dry air at 68 degrees Fahrenheit, sound travels at approximately 343 meters per second, or about 767 miles per hour. If an object exceeds that speed, it breaks the sound barrier, producing a continuous shock wave known as a sonic boom. The first manned aircraft to officially break the sound barrier in level flight was the Bell X-1, piloted by Chuck Yeager in 1947. 

The X-1 was actually modeled after a .50-caliber bullet because engineers knew that specific shape was aerodynamically stable at supersonic speeds. A standard bullet is propelled by the rapid expansion of gases from burning smokeless powder, which replaced black powder in the late 19th century. Black powder is a chemical mixture of sulfur, charcoal, and potassium nitrate, which was historically known as saltpeter. 

Potassium nitrate is heavily used today in agriculture as a fertilizer because it provides two major macronutrients that plants need to survive: potassium and nitrogen. Potassium is an alkali metal, and it's incredibly reactive. If you drop a piece of pure potassium into a bowl of water, it reacts instantly and violently, producing hydrogen gas and generating enough heat to ignite that gas, which burns with a characteristic pale purple flame. Fire itself isn't a state of matter; it's just the visible, tangible effect of the process of combustion, which is a high-temperature exothermic redox chemical reaction between a fuel and an oxidant.

Engines, especially internal combustion engines, rely on a starter motor to get the crankshaft turning. The starter motor is an electric motor that draws a massive amount of current from the car's battery. Batteries store chemical energy and convert it into electrical energy through redox reactions. The most common type of battery in cars is the lead-acid battery, which was invented in 1859 by French physicist Gaston Planté. It's the oldest type of rechargeable battery.

Hydrogen is the most abundant chemical substance in the universe, constituting roughly 75 percent of all baryonic mass. Stars, like our sun, are primarily composed of hydrogen in its plasma state. 

Plasma is one of the four fundamental states of matter, along with solid, liquid, and gas. It's an ionized gas consisting of positive ions and free electrons in proportions resulting in more or less no overall electric charge. Because it's ionized, plasma is highly electrically conductive and responds strongly to electromagnetic fields. The Northern Lights, or Aurora Borealis, are a beautiful natural display of plasma in the Earth's magnetosphere, caused by solar wind interacting with the Earth's magnetic field. The famous double-helix structure of DNA was discovered in the 1950s, and that discovery heavily relied on the X-ray crystallography work of Rosalind Franklin. X-ray crystallography works by measuring the angles and intensities of X-ray beams that are diffracted by a crystal. In astronomy, X-ray telescopes have to be placed outside the Earth's atmosphere, usually on satellites, because the atmosphere absorbs most X-rays coming from space. 

If it didn't, life on Earth would be constantly bombarded by lethal radiation from distant cosmic events like pulsars and supernovas.
